requirement: Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.
rationale:
The skill text appears to say what the requirement asks, but nothing is linked to the requirement as `{impl}` or `{test}`, so the evidence is incomplete.

**What the skills say**
- `assets/skills/habeas-bootstrap-requirements/SKILL.md` (lines 20–26) says "There is no waiver for an uncited function."
- It tells agents to propose an explicit requirement scoped to one area, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all.
- It also tells agents to get the user's agreement, mark the helper with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all`.
- It forbids using an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.
- `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md` (lines 23–29) repeats the guidance. It adds that the requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function.

**Gaps**
- `references` shows only one site for `requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance`: a `{cite}` in `md/reference.md:369`. A cite does not make the skill files inputs to this requirement's review, and the reference page treats cite-only implementation as a gap.
- Neither skill file carries an `{impl}` marker for this requirement. The same is true of the sibling skill requirements, such as `behavior_review_guidance`.
- No test checks the bundled skills' content. Searches of `tests/` for "no waiver", "uncited" and "internal.config_parsing" found nothing, and `src` has no code that references the skill files.
- No FIXME or other source comment acknowledges these gaps.

The requirement is therefore not marked as implemented and not tested. Neither a missing test nor a missing marker is justified by simplicity or impracticality. A simple test could assert that the bundled skills contain the required directives.

text: :::{req} internal_detail_guidance

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.
- `{cite}`: the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition without implementing or testing it.

Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. `{impl}` and `{test}` point from the definition to the source, so the source becomes a mandatory input to the definition's assessment, and that definition's evidence must cover the reference line. `{cite}` points from the source to the definition: a citing requirement or example receives the cited declaration as context, and the citing site needs no evidence coverage. Marking only `{cite}` on code that implements part of a requirement leaves a gap in that requirement's review. In the book, references and definitions become linked badges.
{cite}`requirements.references.targets` {cite}`requirements.references.evidence_coverage` {cite}`requirements.references.authoring_inputs`

For Rust, Habeas parses first-party source files and requires every explicit function or method, including trait methods and test helpers, to have a requirement or named example reference in an attached comment or its body. Each named example references a requirement. A reference on an enclosing `impl` or module, in a string literal, or only in an evidence input does not cover the function. A Rust source file that cannot be parsed is reported as an error. For a helper with no behavior-specific requirement, agree on an explicit internal-detail requirement scoped to one area, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function's behavior; it cannot justify otherwise unspecified user-visible behavior. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_function_coverage` {cite}`requirements.cli.internal_detail_guidance`

Rust-item selectors use syntactic ancestry within one repository-relative file. Examples include `mod[local]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing]/fn[run]`, `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`, `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`, `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`, and positional `use#1`. Duplicate sibling names gain `#1`, `#2`, and so on. Delimiter characters and whitespace within names or impl types use percent-encoded UTF-8 bytes, so spelling can be recovered without resolving modules across files. {cite}`requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`
## Checking and viewing
:::{req} behavior_review_guidance

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents reviewing code against requirements to inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling, and verify both that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and that it introduces no additional end-user-observable behavior without an agreed requirement. They MUST explain the requirement and example review criteria in {cite}`requirements.ci.review_criteria`, including test adequacy and justified absence of tests for requirements, and the three outcomes and documented-gap convention in {cite}`requirements.ci.outcomes`. Agents MUST mark code that implements part of a requirement with `{impl}` and tests that verify it with `{test}`, using `{cite}` only for related code that does neither, under {cite}`requirements.references.targets`. Where requirements interact, agents MUST mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A citation alone MUST NOT count as that explanation.
:::{req} internal_detail_guidance

Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST NOT offer a waiver for an uncited first-party Rust function. When a function serves only as an internal implementation detail and no existing requirement explains it, Habeas's bundled agent skills MUST direct agents to propose an explicit project requirement scoped to one area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all requirement, obtain the user's agreement, mark the function with `{impl}`, and run `habeas author --all` for the harness to assess that requirement's evidence. That assessment MUST account for whether the requirement explains each implementing function's behavior. An internal-detail requirement MUST NOT justify an otherwise unspecified end-user-observable behavior.
:::{req} invocation

`habeas mdbook supports html` MUST succeed, and a support query for another renderer MUST fail. An unknown command or invalid setup option combination MUST fail with a usage message. In particular, `habeas agents` and `habeas setup --install-skills` MUST fail with a usage message.

Put at least one `{test}` reference with a full requirement or example name on each test definition or individual case, naming the definitions the test is designed to verify rather than ones it exercises incidentally. A parameterized test can carry a reference at its case source or generating declaration when that is the only editable source. Add multiple references when a test checks multiple definitions. Do not use one file-level tag to stand in for unrelated tests.

Add a requirement or example reference in a Rust comment attached to each inventoried function or method or within its body. Use `{impl}` where the function itself implements part of a definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case the definition specifies. Calling code that implements a definition does not count. Use `{cite}` only for code that relies on or refers to a definition without implementing or testing it; the cited requirement's review treats cite-only implementing code as a gap. An example must reference a requirement with `{test}` or `{cite}`, so an example reference still traces the function to a requirement. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions. There is no waiver for an uncited function. If no behavior-specific requirement explains an internal helper, propose an explicit requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify unspecified end-user-visible behavior.

Run `habeas author --all` to create requirement and example evidence. Each assessment has its own model conversation. Each requirement's review receives the sources marked `{impl}` or `{test}` for it and can look up every source that references it, so it can find implementing code that is unmarked or only cited. It records delivered source inputs and writes judgments and rationales. The supervising agent must not compose or refresh evidence JSON, determinations, rationales, or snapshots itself, or delegate manual evidence writing to another agent. If authoring configuration or credentials are unavailable, report the blocker instead of substituting hand-written evidence.

Inspect every end-user-observable result and branch, including errors and input handling. Check that the code fulfills each applicable requirement and introduces no additional observable behavior without an agreed requirement. When requirements interact, mark every requirement implemented at the relevant point with `{impl}` and explain how their texts jointly account for the behavior. A reference alone does not explain why a behavior, such as accepting `^C`, is specified.

Every explicit function or method in first-party Rust sources needs its own requirement or example reference in an attached Rust comment or within its body, including trait methods and test helpers. A reference on an enclosing module or `impl` does not cover its functions, and there is no uncited-function waiver. If no existing requirement explains an internal helper, propose a requirement scoped to that area of internal code, such as `internal.config_parsing`, rather than one catch-all, get the user's agreement, and mark the helper with `{impl}`. That requirement's review checks that it explains each implementing function. Do not use an internal-detail requirement to justify otherwise unspecified observable behavior.
